newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Brit Biotech 1st product on target.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Brit Biotech 1st product on target.

text.p: British Biotech Plc said on Wednesday it was on target to launch its first product, a drug to treat acute pancreatitis, in the first quarter of 1998.
In a telephone interview with Reuters, finance director James Noble said the group's strategy is now dominated by pancreatitis drug Lexpifant and cancer compound Marimastat.

"Everything else is much more of a sideshow. They are the nearest to market," said Noble, who brushed aside news that Glaxo Wellcome Plc had dropped work on a British Biotech oral asthma compound. "I don't think you'd find one in a hundred investors who'd invested in us on the strength of that."
The Oxford-based concern, a bellwether for the UK's bustling biotech industry, said first-quarter pretax losses widened to 8.0 million stg from 7.0 million a year before.

Noble said the results of late-stage trials of intravenous Lexipafant on pancreatitis patients will be published in November, with positive results leading to a European Marketing application in the first three months of 1997 and the product potentially on sale a year later.
Noble declined to forecast sales, although British Biotech's brokers, ABN Amro Hoare Govett, predict peak turnover of 300 million stg a year.
He said Phase III results would be crucial in determining whether Lexipafant "saves lives and gets people out of intensive care, or just has a mild effect".
"It is very sensitive to those sort of indications."

November will also see further evidence on anti-cancer compound Marimastat, for which Hoare Govett predicts peak sales of 4.6 billion stg. Raw data on Marimastat will be presented to the European Society of Medical Oncology, including analysis of the drug's effectiveness in stomach, colo-rectal, ovarian and pancreatic cancer. Phase III trials in five cancers are underway or due to begin in the next six months.
Noble hopes to tie up a Japanese partnership for the drug before the end of 1996. "That's looking very good," he said.

He dismissed claims by rival biotech pioneer Scotia Holdings Plc that its anti-cancer compound, EF13, was "at least as good" as Marimastat as "rather odd", and said it was inappropriate to make comparisons from the data used by Scotia.

The company ended the first quarter with cash reserves of 200 million stg. Noble said spending in the year to April would rise sharply to around 40 million stg as it moved drugs towards the market, built new laboratories and consolidated operations on a single site.

British Biotech was one of many biotech companies to go to the market for cash this year. Its controversiual rights issue in July raisd 143 million stg but coincided with a bout of nervousness among biotech investors and sharp falls in share prices.

"What we have seen this year is a tremendous amount of money being raised and perhaps there is a bit of fatigue," Noble said. "The next phase is data from the companies proving that they are worth investing in."
